profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting for an existing proposal to harden a prototype continuous experimentation platform running on a heavy commercial truck fleet before a three-week pilot with a logistics partner. The proposal under review covers remote deployment of experimental software containers, on-vehicle data capture from sensors and CAN-derived signals, buffering and upload over intermittent mobile connectivity, and safeguards intended to keep experiments isolated from safety-critical vehicle functions. The agenda is to judge whether the design is ready for pilot approval, identify gaps in the rollout package, and decide what modifications are needed before sign-off. The expected outcome is a shared decision on whether the design is 'pilot-ready' with a short list of follow-up actions.

members.name: Lina Berg
members.expertise: distributed vehicle software platforms, edge deployment, telemetry pipelines
members.background: Lina led the internal prototype of the truck-based experimentation platform and previously built over-the-air update systems for industrial IoT devices; she now reviews platform designs across embedded and cloud boundaries.
members.private_state: She wants the review to end with conditional approval so the team can keep the pilot date with the logistics partner, and she is especially concerned about avoiding any request that would force a redesign of the vehicle-side deployment stack.
hidden_assumptions: If an experiment is described as 'isolated,' it means the code runs in user-space on the secondary compute unit and cannot send commands onto safety-critical buses, even if it still reads mirrored vehicle data.

A 'pilot-ready' design means architecture, interfaces, failure handling, and operational guardrails are sufficiently specified; minor instrumentation and dashboard details can be completed during the first week of the pilot.

The 'rollback path' is the remote ability to disable or replace an experiment container on the next successful mobile check-in, because the baseline production vehicle software itself is not being updated in this pilot.
When the proposal mentions 'the gateway,' it refers to the telematics edge gateway mounted in the truck that brokers upload/download between the experiment node and the cloud.

members.name: Markus Feld
members.expertise: automotive safety cases, verification planning, fleet trial readiness
members.background: Markus has spent most of his career reviewing validation evidence for embedded vehicle features and recently moved into assessing how experimental software can be trialed on public-road commercial vehicles without undermining established safety processes.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid being seen as blocking experimentation, but he also wants enough evidence and operational discipline that the pilot cannot later be criticized as an uncontrolled public-road test.
hidden_assumptions: If an experiment is described as 'isolated,' it means not only no actuation authority but also no possibility of affecting shared compute, network bandwidth, storage, or diagnostic behavior in ways that could interfere with validated vehicle functions.

A design is only 'pilot-ready' when the complete operational package is in place, including concrete acceptance thresholds, monitoring views, escalation paths, and driver-support procedures for field incidents.

A 'rollback path' means the system can be returned to the validated baseline immediately enough to manage a field issue during the same operating shift, not merely after the next successful network contact.
When people refer to 'the gateway,' he assumes they mean the backend ingestion gateway in the cloud through which all fleet data is normalized and made visible to reviewers.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the experimental workload is 'isolated from safety-critical functions.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means process and network isolation sufficient to prevent any command path into safety-critical ECUs; contention on shared non-safety resources is a separate performance concern, not part of the isolation claim.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a stronger notion of isolation that also excludes meaningful interference through CPU contention, disk exhaustion, network saturation, or diagnostic side effects on validated vehicle behavior.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In automotive software reviews, 'isolation' is a familiar positive term and both participants assume the other shares their professional shorthand; because both are supportive of separation in principle, neither feels a need to unpack the boundary of the term.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to checks and limits being enforced 'at the gateway.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the on-vehicle telematics gateway that schedules uploads, receives deployment bundles, and mediates connectivity for the experiment node.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the cloud ingestion gateway that validates incoming data packages, enforces fleet-side policy, and feeds the monitoring portal used in review.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both systems are legitimately called gateways in the current program documentation, and in a design review each person hears the term in the layer they work with most; because the sentence still sounds correct either way, the ambiguity survives.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both evaluate whether the proposal is 'pilot-ready.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks pilot-ready means the core architecture and remote operations are safe enough to begin the limited fleet trial, with some observability refinements and reporting views allowed to mature during the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks pilot-ready means the end-to-end trial package is complete before any truck goes live, including reviewed runbooks, alert thresholds, driver contact procedures, and evidence that field staff can interpret anomalies.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Readiness language is common in approval meetings and often left intentionally high-level; both participants are used to saying something is ready 'with actions,' so the stricter versus looser acceptance threshold remains hidden.

misalignment_points.topic: How rollback is expected to work
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the design needs a 'rollback path' for experiments.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes rollback is executed by sending a disable or replacement package that the truck applies at the next heartbeat when connectivity is available, with local watchdogs keeping the baseline services running meanwhile.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes rollback involves a field-operational method to revert the experiment during an active route window, effectively near-immediate from an operational perspective, even under weak connectivity conditions.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both endorse rollback as an obvious safeguard, but each silently imports a different operational timescale from their background; since neither disputes the need for rollback itself, they do not naturally drill into the exact mechanism and latency.

turns.inner_thought: I need to set the frame clearly: this is a narrow pilot, not a platform re-architecture discussion. Two tractors, three weeks, remote container deployment onto the secondary compute unit, local buffering, mirrored vehicle data, uploads when connectivity allows. If I keep the scope grounded, Markus is less likely to ask for changes that touch the vehicle-side deployment stack.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making the time. At a high level, what we're reviewing is a limited public-road pilot on two truck tractors over three weeks. The proposal covers remote deployment of experiment containers, local buffering on the vehicle, capture of selected signals for post-run analysis, and the guardrails around how that all operates with intermittent connectivity. The question today is whether that package is in shape for the logistics-partner pilot and, if not, what the minimum actions are before sign-off.

turns.inner_thought: I want to sound constructive, not like the safety person who always says no. But for me pilot-ready means the full operational package is complete before trucks go live: thresholds, monitoring, escalation, driver contact, review visibility. If daily operation isn't properly framed, this can later be criticized as an uncontrolled road test.
turns.utterance: Yes, exactly. From my side the review goal is pretty simple: decide whether this is pilot-ready for day-to-day operation on public roads without leaving us exposed to uncontrolled field risk. If there are gaps, I'd rather make them explicit now and tie them to concrete actions than discover them in the first week.

turns.inner_thought: The strongest point is that the experiment runs in user space on the secondary box, reads mirrored signals, and has no route to command safety-critical buses. That's what isolated from safety-critical functions means here. Shared resource tuning matters, but it's not the core architectural question and I don't want the term expanded into a redesign demand.
turns.utterance: On the key safety point, the experiment workload is isolated from safety-critical functions. It runs on the secondary compute side, it only receives mirrored signals, and there isn't an actuation path from the experiment back into the vehicle control domain. So the separation principle in the proposal is the same one we used in the prototype, just with tighter deployment and logging controls.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds directionally right, but isolated from safety-critical functions has to cover interference channels too. I need confidence the experiment can't starve shared CPU, fill storage, flood the bus with diagnostics, or otherwise perturb validated behavior indirectly. I'll ask without making it sound adversarial.
turns.utterance: I’m aligned that isolation is the right starting point. What I want to make sure of for public-road use is that the same claim holds under less tidy conditions as well—load spikes, storage growth, unexpected diagnostic traffic, that kind of thing. Are those bounded tightly enough in the current package?

turns.inner_thought: He’s asking about rates and controls; that's fine. The important answer is that the telematics edge gateway on the truck shapes uploads and only accepts deployment pulls during scheduled windows. Saying it's enforced at the gateway should be enough and keeps us away from arguing about internals on the node.
turns.utterance: Yes, those controls are part of the proposal. The rate limits are enforced at the gateway, uploads are shaped around the available mobile link, and deployment pulls only happen in scheduled windows rather than opportunistically. So the intent is that the experiment flow stays predictable even when connectivity is messy.

turns.inner_thought: Good, if the backend ingestion gateway is doing those checks and policy enforcement, then auditability should be straightforward. For my purposes, reviewers need visibility into malformed payloads, rejected packages, and policy violations in the monitoring portal before I call this complete enough.
turns.utterance: That helps. If those checks and limits are enforced at the gateway, then from an audit point of view we should be in decent shape, provided the monitoring makes them visible. I’d want reviewers to be able to see malformed packets, policy rejections, and similar events in the pilot dashboard rather than having that buried in engineering logs.

turns.inner_thought: Here's the approval move: assert pilot-ready based on architecture, deployment flow, buffering, and remote disable. The richer dashboard can land during week one; that's normal. And rollback path, as far as I’m concerned, is the remote disable or replacement package on next check-in, with baseline services unaffected because they're already resident on the vehicle.
turns.utterance: My view is that the design is pilot-ready because the core mechanics are there already: deployment flow, local buffering, containment boundaries, and remote disable controls. The richer operations dashboard is still a follow-up task, but I see that as polish around the pilot rather than a blocker to starting it.

turns.inner_thought: I can support 'pilot-ready with actions' only if pilot-ready still implies complete operational discipline before go-live: field runbooks, thresholds, escalation chain, driver-support steps, and a rollback path usable during a live shift. I need to state that expectation without sounding like I'm moving the goalposts.
turns.utterance: I can get comfortable with that framing if pilot-ready still includes the operational basics being nailed down: field runbooks, alert thresholds, who gets called when something looks wrong, and a rollback path that operations can rely on during a live shift. That’s the part that tends to matter once the trucks are actually out earning money.

turns.inner_thought: No issue, we have a rollback path: send a disable package, truck applies it at the next successful heartbeat, experiment container stops or is replaced, baseline vehicle software keeps running because we're not updating it in this pilot. I should present that confidently and keep it matter-of-fact.
turns.utterance: On rollback, the mechanism in the proposal is to push a disable package so the truck drops the experiment at the next successful heartbeat. The baseline services on the vehicle continue as they are, so we’re not depending on any broader software reversion in order to get back to the normal state.

turns.inner_thought: All right, there is a rollback path, and I don't want to derail the meeting by unpacking timing unless I have to. But from my perspective the logistics partner will assume that means operationally quick enough within the same shift, even with poor motorway coverage. I should register that expectation gently.
turns.utterance: Understood. Having that rollback path is important, and I think the logistics partner will mainly care that if something looks problematic, it can be cleared quickly in operational terms even with patchy coverage on the route. As long as we capture that expectation in the package, I’m not trying to overcomplicate it.

turns.inner_thought: He's still broadly onside. I should push toward conditional approval now: architecture and safeguards are settled, and the remaining work is the incident playbook plus reviewer-facing views. If we label those as actions before the first data review, we keep the pilot date without reopening platform design.
turns.utterance: Then my proposal would be approval with actions. I think the architecture and the main safeguards are settled well enough for the pilot, and the remaining items are to finish the incident playbook and the reviewer-facing views before the first formal data review. That gets us moving without pretending there’s no follow-through work left.

turns.inner_thought: I can agree in principle if the notes explicitly record the evidence I care about: checks at the gateway, support for the isolation claim, and rollback steps the field team can follow. I still mean the cloud gateway, broader interference evidence, and an operationally immediate rollback path, but nothing she's said has contradicted that on the surface.
turns.utterance: That sounds reasonable to me in principle. If we capture the gateway checks, the isolation evidence, and the rollback steps clearly in the review notes—and tie the operational items to named actions—I’d expect the pilot can move forward on that basis.
